title: Tuples and deconstruction
body: A tuple groups a few values without declaring a type: `(string Name, int Score) best = ("Ada", 97);`. Tuples are value types (`System.ValueTuple`), so assignment copies them. Element names are compile-time conveniences; the underlying fields are `Item1`, `Item2`.

Methods can return several values as a tuple: `static (int Min, int Max) Range(int[] xs)`. That is often clearer than out parameters. When a grouping gets a name and behaviour, promote it to a record.

Deconstruction unpacks a tuple or any type with a `Deconstruct` method into variables: `var (min, max) = Range(data);`. Use `_` to discard elements you do not need. Deconstruction also enables swapping without a temporary: `(a, b) = (b, a);`.
Tuples support `==` and `!=` element by element, and they make convenient composite keys for dictionaries and switch expressions (`(x, y) switch { (0, 0) => ... }`).

Tuple element names do not participate in type identity: `(int A, int B)` and `(int X, int Y)` convert to each other silently. Check that positional order, not just names, matches when passing tuples between methods.
challenge: Write a method Stats(int[] xs) returning (int Count, double Mean) and deconstruct the result for [2, 4, 9], printing the mean with one decimal.
question: What does `(a, b) = (b, a);` do?
wrong: Creates a new tuple but leaves a and b unchanged
reasoning: The right-hand tuple is built first from the old values, then deconstructed into a and b.
